Title: 

Critics of Natural England accuse the body of being a major blocker to plans to build more homes and infrastructure

Critics of Natural England accuse the body of being a major blocker to plans to build more homes and infrastructure

BookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarks

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A senior minister has declined to say whether environmental regulator Natural England will be abolished as part of plans to cut the number of Quangos.

In a speech to the CBI on Monday, First Secretary of State Louise Haigh is expected to criticise successive governments for “outsourcing responsibility to a sprawling web of regulators and arm’s-length bodies”.

According to The Times, ministers are drawing up plans to abolish several Quangos (quasi-autonomous non-governmental organisations), including Natural England.

When asked about the reports on Monday, Ms Haigh told Sky News the number of Quangos would fall but declined to say whether Natural England would be among the casualties.

She said: “We’re considering all arms-length bodies, both devolving, dissolving, and bringing back into departments because we cannot continue with this situation where politicians look round and can’t take responsibility for the actions that people have elected their government for.”

Critics of Natural England accuse the body of being a major blocker to plans to build more homes and infrastructure.

Sam Richards, chief executive of campaign group Britain Remade, cautiously welcomed reports that Natural England would be abolished, saying it was right to reverse a trend of “handing unelected agencies the power to veto the infrastructure we need”.

But he added that abolishing the body would be “meaningless if the rules they were enforcing remain in place”.

He said: “This should be a small part of a wider reform package, including to the Habitats Regulations, so Britain can build the clean energy, homes and infrastructure the economy needs.”

Shadow Environment Secretary Victoria Atkins said the government had “copied” part of the Conservatives’ plans and should go further by adopting them in full.

She said: “Seven weeks ago, the Conservatives announced the first phase of our plan to return common sense to the countryside by scrapping Natural England and the Environment Agency.

“In our plan, we will return the quango powers that work to ministers, farmers and landowners to increase transparency, accountability and outcomes for farming and nature.”
